title: Noctua finds more than half of PC cases misstate CPU cooler clearances

Noctua
is known for making high-end, high-quality fans and air coolers, which it has been doing
for over 20 years
, recently
expanding into AIOs
. However, it appears that there were a few questions regarding its PC case compatibility database, which some PC DIYers say don’t match the data from the manufacturer’s website. The company cleared this up in a
blog post
, saying that it has undertaken its own measurements and it has determined that 56 of the more than 100 cases it has tested showed significant deviation from the details officially listed online.
The company gave two diverging situations of inaccurate official measurements. The first one is when the case is larger than what is actually written, which would allow PC builders to attach a larger cooler. Noctua said that the deviations aren’t minor, either. For example, the NZXT H2 Flow case is listed as being compatible with a maximum 75mm CPU cooler height, but the actual case can accommodate an air cooler up to 79mm. There’s also the
Thermaltake
TR100, which is 2.7mm larger than what the Thermaltake website says, and the Corsair Frame 4000D, which gives you 10mm of extra clearance.
This is a good thing, as any cooler you bought based on their website’s measurement means that it will definitely fit, but Noctua said that this is a missed opportunity. That’s because you could’ve bought a larger cooler that delivered more performance in the same case.

On the flip side, the company warned that there were also some cases that were actually smaller versus the numbers in their specifications. It cited two examples — the Asus Prime AP201 and the Lian Li B4-mATX. The former is 1.7mm shorter while the latter is 3.5mm shorter than what’s listed on their specific product pages.
This could to be a major issue, especially if you bought items that fitted the available space exactly, based on the manufacturer’s measurements. It would mean that these parts would either be touching the case panels, or worse, not allow them to close at all. If that’s the case, you’ll have to spend extra effort to return either the part or the case and get something that fits better.
The safest solution to this is for you to buy the PC case before you shop for the remaining parts of your build. This is especially true if you’re looking at the
best mini-ITX cases
, as the tight tolerances mean that you don’t have much margin if the numbers aren’t accurate. But by having the case physically available and measuring it yourself, you’re at least confident that what you’re buying will fit. Alternatively, you can check out
Noctua’s compatibility search
page, with the clearances of the cases in its database verified by its team.
This compatibility tool will give you peace of mind when
shopping for the best cooler
and is useful for confirming measurements even if you end up buying from another brand. But this begs the question — are the variations between official and actual measurements limited to the air coolers? Or are the numbers for other components, like the GPU, PSU, and other key components also inaccurate? Noctua’s website only covers coolers, so you’ll have to rely on other pages (or your own measurements) if you want some confirmation of a case’s specifications and clearances for other parts like GPUs and PSUs.

I can somewhat understand case manufacturers lowballing the measurements as there are plenty of different platforms which can be used and no guarantee how cooler height is measured. In some cases it may also be that the cooler height doesn't particularly matter (the Frame 4000D for example has a rated height of 170mm which is already enough for every cooler Noctua sells). Getting it wrong from the other direction though has a much higher chance of being a problem.
Smaller cases are the wildcard in this as both being wrong has the potential to be a problem. The tolerances being tighter can be a tricky thing and every mm can matter (my Deskmini "supports" 47mm coolers and I did get it to fit, but it was hard to get the side over it and it presses against). Small differences could mean a difference between cooler classifications. Sometimes even here though the measurements don't necessarily mean much though. In their example of the H2 Flow the case is designed for liquid cooling and has a glass panel over the socket restricting air cooler use so the extra space isn't enough to fit a better cooler.

comment.text:
If errors of over half a typical screwhole width are so common, why has it never been noticed before and reported on?

That seems literally impossible to not notice for years on end.

Noctua doesnt seem like they would put up fake data either… so does that imply the rest of the industry and supply chain are full of fakers?

It depends on the reference data, case companies are of course good at measuring these things given everything that needs to match up when building a PC to begin with. Therefore I would assume that case manufacturers measure it but add on an amount for assured clearance.

However of course it matters for Noctua as they want their coolers to fit and be assured they can fit into common/popular cases.

My thoughts are that if you take a case and a cooler, the assumption needs to include AMD and intel sockets and potentially multiple different generations of both that may have a sizeable difference in height between each other. Unless you take your measurement from the thickest of those as a safety net. A quick Google says that they can vary between +/-3mm typically.

There's no obvious datum to reference, for starters.

From bottom to top you've got the motherboard tray, standoff spacers, the motherboard itself, the socket, the CPU itself, the cooler, and finally the side plate of the case.

For most parts the top of the motherboard is the easiest reference. Motherboards are usually ~1.57mm thick, which gives the case manufacturer a pretty solid reference for the placement of the rear io shield, PCIe cutouts, and motherboard spacer length.

Now, the case manufacturer knows how wide the case is, so they know the distance from the top of the (expected) motherboard to the side panel. That's easy. But that's not the cooler height - you need to subtract the height of the socket and the CPU from that. How much is that? That's going to vary from socket to socket! Intel's LGA1851 has a stack-up height of 7.03 +- 0.5mm, AMD's AM5 is 7.98 +- 0.6mm. So currently it is anywhere from 6.53mm to 8.58mm - which isn't very helpful if you're asked to write a spec sheet...

So what is a case manufacturer to do? It doesn't hurt to have a bit of extra space, so you're probably going to have some kind of historic "maximum socket height" value lying around which you just subtract from the top-of-motherboard clearance to determine cooler clearance - as you have been doing for decades. It's not true but it's close enough, and nobody complains so why would the case manufacturer care? Or you physically measure it, and end up with a skewed measurement because you accidentally measured on a very thin Intel CPU / very fat AMD CPU.

TL;DR: Nobody notices because it is nontrivial to determine, and very few people care about squeezing out every last millimeter of cooler clearance.

> very few people care about squeezing out every last millimeter of cooler clearance

I believe that may not be entirely true, given the recent interest in DIY cheap steam boxes that are packed to the millimeter with fan cooling. While it’s not necessarily an eATX solution, certainly there is at least medium demand for knowing case tolerances within a millimeter these days. 5mm of extra fan thickness gives you something like +10-20% CFM, which can be a performance-limiting factor in these custom builds:
